claims.text: Dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes is governed by the interaction between stacking-fault energy and dislocation activity.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes twinning-mediated plasticity in FeNiCrMn.
Higher strain rates and lower temperatures favor twinning-mediated plasticity in FeNiCrMn.
Twinning-mediated plasticity enhances the strength–ductility balance.
The target material is solidified, Co-free FeNiCrMn with equiatomic or near-equiatomic proportions.
Temperature and strain rate will be varied during tension or compression testing.
The proposed tests span cryogenic to elevated temperatures and quasi-static to high strain rates.
Stacking-fault energy influences dislocation activity and deformation twinning.
At lower stacking-fault energy, twinning enhances strain hardening and ductility under dynamic conditions.
At higher stacking-fault energy, dislocation slip dominates deformation.
FeNiCrMn will show increased strain hardening at lower temperatures and higher strain rates because of twinning-mediated plasticity.
FeNiCrMn will show increased ductility at lower temperatures and higher strain rates because of twinning-mediated plasticity.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, dislocation slip will dominate and strain hardening will be lower.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, ductility will be lower.
The hypothesis is limited to Co-free FeNiCrMn alloys with similar microstructures and excludes significant composition or processing-induced variations.
The exact stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrMn and its variation with temperature and strain rate are not well established.
A transition from twinning-mediated plasticity at low temperature and high strain rate to dislocation-dominated deformation at high temperature and low strain rate is required by the hypothesis.
